title: A Guest from Germany
text:
Last September my family agreed to take in an exchange student for one semester. We had never been a [[host]] family before, and my mother cleaned the whole house twice.

Our [[guest]] was a quiet sixteen-year-old girl called Lena. On her first day at school, our teacher asked her to [[introduce]] herself to the class, and her voice shook the whole time.

For the first two weeks she was [[homesick]]. She missed her parents so much that she cried on the phone with them every night. She would also [[apologize]] every time she used the wrong Chinese word, even though nobody minded.

So we tried to make her feel at home. My grandmother taught her to make a [[traditional]] sweet soup that Taiwanese families have eaten at the Lantern Festival for hundreds of years, and she learned to [[greet]] our neighbors in Taiwanese with "Have you eaten yet?", which made the old men downstairs laugh with delight.

By November she was a [[regular]] customer at the dumpling shop on our corner, eating there three times a week. At home my grandmother would [[praise]] her in front of the whole family, saying her dumplings were better than mine. Living abroad also made her more [[independent]]; by the end she could take the train to Hualien by herself.

She even became so [[skillful]] with chopsticks that she could pick up a single peanut. Her family's dinner time, she told us, was [[similar]] to ours: just as loud, just as long and just as full of arguments about nothing.

At our farewell dinner she said she would always [[admire]] the way my grandmother worked from morning to night. "I want you to know how much I [[appreciate]] everything," she said, and this time it was my mother who cried.

Next summer I will be the [[visitor]], and she has already planned where to take me first.

title: Lost at the Night Market
text:
Last Saturday the night market near our school was so [[crowded]] that we could barely move, and so loud that I had to shout to my friend standing next to me.

I was waiting for my bubble tea when I noticed a little boy standing all [[alone]] next to a fruit stand. He was about four years old, and he was crying so hard that he could not speak.

His mother, I learned later, had looked away for one second, and he seemed to [[disappear]] into the crowd. I knelt down and spoke in a soft voice, because I did not want to [[frighten]] him even more. He did not [[trust]] me at first, and he kept his hands behind his back.

A woman who was a regular [[customer]] at the fruit stand said she had seen his mother earlier. A small crowd began to [[gather]] around us, and everyone had a different idea. I wanted to shout the mother's name, but in all that noise nobody would hear me.

I could have walked away, but I would [[rather]] wait with him than leave him with strangers. Nobody else was helping, and I felt [[responsible]] for keeping him safe. So I called the police. Two officers arrived within ten minutes, and one of them knelt down to [[calm]] the boy with a red balloon.

Then there was a sudden shout behind us. A young woman pushing a stroller came running toward us. She had been searching for almost an hour, and her phone had died.

The boy jumped into her arms. She thanked me again and again and called me a [[hero]], which made my face turn red. I am eighteen now, and I only did what any [[adult]] should do.

title: Grandpa's Old Record Player
text:
When my grandfather moved in with us last spring, he brought two boxes: one of clothes, and one with an old record player and fifty records.

To me, the machine looked almost [[ancient]], like something from a museum. It was brown and heavy, and it did not even have a screen. To most people it would be just an [[ordinary]] old machine, but my grandmother had bought it for him in 1978.

Most of his records were [[classical]] music — Bach, Mozart and Chopin — but a few were [[rare]] Taiwanese songs that you cannot find online, so last month I helped him [[upload]] three of them to the Internet. He loves the way those old songs [[mix]] Taiwanese and Japanese words in a single line.

Every evening after dinner he sits in his chair and stays completely [[silent]] for an hour, without saying a single word. At first I could not [[imagine]] how anyone could listen to one piece from beginning to end without checking a phone.

Then one night he asked me to stop the record in the middle of a piano piece and tell him what I heard. I said, "Nothing." He played it again and taught me to [[focus]] on one instrument at a time. This time I heard rain inside the music.

He says he does not [[regret]] anything about growing old, except that his hands now shake too much to change the records. So that is my job.

Last week the needle broke. My father said we should just [[recycle]] the old machine and buy a modern speaker. My grandfather said nothing, but I could see in his eyes how precious those records were to him — not because of money, but because of my grandmother.

I finally found a new needle through a [[former]] music teacher who now repairs old machines. Those evenings have made me want to learn the piano myself.
